opus-5.5.text:
I think "generalization" gets used very loosely, so I'd break it into a few layers.

The first layer is interpolation: the model has seen many similar things, and it can smoothly fill in the gaps between them. Honestly, most of what impresses people falls into this category. With enough data and a good enough architecture, interpolation already looks a lot like magic. But I wouldn't call it true generalization in the deeper sense.

The second layer is compositional generalization: the model has learned A and learned B separately, and when you ask for A and B together, something it has probably never seen, it can still produce something reasonable. Here I've seen real progress, especially in generative models. You can combine concepts, styles, and physical situations in ways that clearly weren't in the training data, and the result still holds together. That tells me the model has learned something structured, not just memorized surface patterns.

The third layer, which I care about most, is whether the model has learned the underlying rules of how the world works. If you put it in a new environment or give it a new kind of interaction, does it still behave consistently? Does an object stay the same object when the camera moves away and comes back? Does cause come before effect? At this layer my honest assessment is that we're still early. Models can look very convincing over short horizons, but when you push them longer, or into the long tail, consistency starts to break down. That's often where you discover the model was relying on statistical shortcuts rather than real understanding.

So my overall view is cautious optimism. Scaling clearly buys generalization, more than many of us expected a few years ago. But I don't think scale alone closes the last gap. We need better ways to evaluate generalization, not just benchmarks that are secretly close to the training distribution, and we probably need training signals that come from interaction rather than passive observation. When a model has to act and live with the consequences, it can't get away with shortcuts as easily. I think that's where the next real jump in generalization will come from.

r001.rationale: The response discusses interpolation, compositional generalization, and consistency in new environments, but it does not identify positional generalization as the kind demonstrated by the model examples.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, generalization is the thing that surprised us the most, and it's also the thing I'm most careful about when talking to people.

When we trained the earlier versions, we built the data pipeline around a fairly narrow set of scenarios: human portraits, common objects, a handful of indoor scenes. So my expectation was that the model would do well inside that distribution and fall apart the moment you stepped outside. That's what every GAN we trained before did. You'd give it a slightly unusual pose and the whole image would collapse.

What actually happened with the diffusion-based models is different. We'd feed in prompts and conditions that nobody on the team had ever written during data construction, and the model would produce something coherent. Not perfect, but coherent. Combinations of concepts that never co-occurred in the training set. That's the part that made me rethink what "generalization" even means here. It's not interpolating between memorized samples anymore. It's more like the model has learned some compositional structure, and it can recombine pieces it has seen into things it hasn't.

But I want to be precise, because there's a lot of hype. There are two kinds of generalization and we only have one of them.

The first is what I'd call surface generalization: new styles, new combinations, new viewpoints. The model is very strong at this. The second is what I'd call physical or causal generalization: does it understand that a glass dropped from a table will break, that a shadow has to be consistent with the light source, that hands have five fingers and the fingers bend in one direction. Here it's much weaker. It gets these right statistically, because the training data overwhelmingly shows them right, but when you push into a corner case you discover there's no underlying model of the world. It's pattern matching at a very high level of abstraction, and I'd be lying if I said it's reasoning.

So how do I assess it? I look less at benchmark numbers and more at failure modes. If the failures are random, that tells me the model is close to its capacity limit. If the failures are systematic, say the model always gets reflections wrong in the same way, that tells me there's a missing concept, and that's where the next round of data or architecture work should go. Right now most of our failures are systematic, which, to me, is actually good news. It means there's a roadmap.

And one more thing I've come to believe. A lot of what looks like generalization is really data coverage we underestimated. The internet is very large. When the model does something "new," the first question I ask is whether it's actually new or whether we just never looked at that slice of the data. Half the time it's the latter. So I'm optimistic, but I try to stay humble about how much of it is the model and how much of it is the data.

r001.rationale: The response mentions unusual poses and new viewpoints, but does not clearly identify positional generalization—generalizing to new object positions or spatial arrangements—as the demonstrated capability.

astra-6.text:
I think the generalization we’ve seen is encouraging, but we need to be precise about what we mean by generalization. A model can perform well on examples that look new to us but are still very close to patterns it encountered during training. That’s different from handling a genuinely unfamiliar situation.

What interests me most is whether the model can take concepts it has learned and combine them appropriately in a new context. When it does that consistently, it’s a stronger signal than a few impressive examples. But I would still look at where it fails: Does a small change in the input break the result? Does the performance hold when the setting changes? So my assessment is optimistic, but I wouldn’t equate impressive demonstrations with reliable generalization.

r001.rationale: The response discusses combining learned concepts in new contexts, but it does not identify positional generalization as the kind demonstrated by the examples.

sol-6.1.text: I think it depends on what we mean by generalization. A model can perform well on examples similar to its training data, but that doesn’t necessarily mean it can handle a new setting or a new combination of concepts. What I find encouraging is when it can apply something it has learned in a context it hasn’t seen before. But I would still be cautious: a few impressive examples aren’t enough. We need to understand where it succeeds, where it fails, and how consistently it behaves as the task changes.
